facts.text: Grade is the steepness of the ground; downhill travel reduces available machine deceleration, while uphill travel increases it.
facts.quote: Grade is the steepness of the ground; going downhill reduces how hard a machine can slow down, and going uphill helps it.

facts.text: Grade is usually expressed as a percentage: a 10 percent grade rises or falls 1 m for every 10 m traveled, while a 20 percent grade is 1 in 5.
facts.quote: Grade is usually given as a percentage: a 10 percent grade rises or falls 1 m for every 10 m traveled, and 20 percent, common on haul roads and ramps, is 1 in 5.

facts.text: A 20 percent grade is common on haul roads and ramps.
facts.quote: 20 percent, common on haul roads and ramps

facts.text: Gravity adds or removes acceleration of g × sin θ along a slope, where g is 9.81 m/s² and θ is the slope angle; for job-site grades, sin θ is approximately the grade fraction.
facts.quote: gravity adds or removes an acceleration of g x sin θ along the slope, where g is 9.81 m/s² and θ is the slope angle. For job-site grades sin θ is almost the grade fraction

facts.text: A 10 percent downgrade reduces available deceleration by about 1.0 m/s², and a 20 percent downgrade reduces it by about 1.9 m/s².
facts.quote: a 10 percent downgrade costs about 1.0 m/s² and a 20 percent downgrade about 1.9 m/s².

facts.text: Heavy machines can deliver deceleration of 0.6 to 3 m/s².
facts.quote: the 0.6 to 3 m/s² heavy machines can deliver at all

facts.text: Grade and payload shift available heavy-machine deceleration by the same order as the deceleration itself.
facts.quote: grade and payload "shift available deceleration by the same order as the deceleration itself" [Chapter 8].

facts.text: In the New South Wales 100 t truck example, the grade correction alone is about 1.04 m/s², exceeding the 0.75 m/s² net safe deceleration being tested.
facts.quote: In the New South Wales 100 t truck example the grade correction alone is about 1.04 m/s², larger than the 0.75 m/s² net safe deceleration being tested [Chapter 8].

facts.text: A stopping model from the US National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) found combinations in which downhill pull exceeded brake capacity and the simulated machine did not stop at all.
facts.quote: A NIOSH stopping model (NIOSH is the US National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health) found combinations where the downhill pull exceeded brake capacity and the simulated machine did not stop at all.

entities.name: National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health

facts.text: A 2015 road simulation compared braking triggers that ignored and included grade; the grade-blind trigger avoided collision on level ground but collided at grades of 11 and 17 percent.
facts.quote: A road simulation from 2015 compared a braking trigger that ignored grade with one that included it: the grade-blind trigger avoided the collision on level ground and collided at 11 and 17 percent [Chapter 8].

facts.text: A machine stopped on a grade can roll back when the automatic brake releases.
facts.quote: Slopes also bring rollback: a machine stopped on a grade can move again when the automatic brake releases

facts.text: ISO 21815-3 recommends an operator action, such as applying the parking brake, before automatic brake release on a grade to address rollback risk.
facts.quote: so ISO 21815-3 recommends an operator action, such as applying the parking brake, before release [Chapter 8].

facts.text: Side slopes add a tipping risk during braking.
facts.quote: Side slopes add a tipping risk during braking.

facts.text: Grade must be an input to the braking decision and trigger model, rather than a correction applied afterwards.
facts.quote: Grade must be an input to the braking decision, not a correction applied afterwards: "grade belongs in the trigger model" [Chapter 8].

facts.text: The published South African closed-loop test specification uses gradients of 1 percent or less and unloaded machines.
facts.quote: The published South African closed-loop test specification is run on gradients of 1 percent or less and unloaded

facts.text: Slope and loaded cases are not covered by any published specification, according to the booklet.
facts.quote: so slope and loaded cases are not covered by any published specification [Chapter 7].
